opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I don't think the answer is purely one or the other.

Historically, robotics has mostly gone the specialized route. If you look at industrial arms in car factories, or warehouse robots, they're extremely good at one thing, in a very structured environment. And that works. The economics work. But the problem is that every new task becomes a new engineering project. You redesign the hardware, you rewrite the software, you re-tune everything. It doesn't scale to the long tail of things people actually want robots to do in homes, in offices, in the messy real world.

What's changed in the last few years is really on the intelligence side. With large models, foundation models, we're starting to see that a single model trained on a lot of diverse data can generalize across tasks in a way that hand-engineered systems never could. Once you believe that, the question becomes: what body should that brain live in? And the argument for humanoids is that the world is built for humans. Doors, stairs, tools, kitchens, all of it is designed around the human form. So if you want one robot that can go anywhere and do many things, the human form factor is a very natural choice. There's also a data argument: there's an enormous amount of video of humans doing things, and the closer the robot's body is to ours, the easier it potentially is to learn from that data.

That said, I'm pragmatic about it. Humanoids are hard. Balance, safety, cost, reliability, all of these are still open challenges. A wheeled base with two arms might get you eighty percent of the usefulness at a fraction of the complexity for many settings. So my view is that the intelligence should be general, and that's where I'd place the big bet. The embodiment can be more flexible. Ideally you have a model that can control many different bodies, humanoid, quadruped, arms, and it transfers what it learns across them.

So I'd say: general-purpose is the goal, and I think it's achievable in a way it wasn't ten years ago. But on the path there, specialized deployments are valuable, because they're how you get robots into the real world, collect real data, and learn what actually breaks. The two strategies aren't really in competition; one feeds the other.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've gone back and forth on a lot, honestly. Let me try to lay out how I think about it.

The case for specialization is very practical. If you pick one domain, say warehouse logistics, or a quadruped doing inspection, you can constrain the problem. The environment is semi-structured, the task distribution is narrow, you can engineer around failure modes, and you can actually ship something that works today. A lot of the robots that are generating real value right now are specialized, and I don't think that's an accident.

But the reason I keep coming back to the general-purpose direction is what we learned from language models. For years, people in NLP built separate systems for translation, for summarization, for question answering, and each one was a separate research program. Then it turned out that training one large model on everything made all of them better, and the model learned things nobody explicitly designed for. I think the same positive transfer exists in robotics. Picking up a cup and opening a drawer and walking across a room share a lot of underlying structure: perception, physical common sense, how objects respond to contact. If you build ten separate robots, you learn those ten times and you never get to amortize.

The humanoid form factor specifically, I'd separate from the general-purpose question. You can be general-purpose on a wheeled base with two arms. The argument for humanoid is mostly about the world being designed for humans, stairs, door handles, counter heights, and about data, because human video is the largest source of embodied data we have, and the closer your morphology is to a person, the easier that transfer becomes. That argument is real, but the legged locomotion adds a lot of cost and difficulty, so I don't think it's a slam dunk.

My honest view is that the dichotomy is a bit false. The way I'd do it is to build the general foundation model, the shared brain, and then deploy it through specialized products. The specialized deployments are where you collect real data, where you find out what actually fails, and that data flows back and makes the general model better. What I'd be worried about is a team that goes fully general with no deployment, because then you're training on simulation and teleoperation forever and never closing the loop with the real world. And I'd equally worry about a team so specialized that nothing they learn carries over to the next problem.

So, generality as the research direction and the long-term bet, specialization as the path to data and revenue. The teams that figure out how to do both at once are the ones I think will win.

r002.rationale: It says training one large language model improved several tasks, but does not claim generalist models surpassed specialized language models.

r003.rationale: It explicitly cites lessons from language models, including positive transfer from one model trained across tasks, as a reason to pursue general-purpose robotics.

astra-6.text:
I think the long-term goal is general-purpose robots, but the practical path is to start with specific applications. Those two things are not necessarily in conflict.

A humanoid has the potential to do many different tasks in environments designed for people. But having that form factor doesn’t automatically give you general intelligence or the reliability needed to be useful. You still need to solve concrete problems and do them well.

So I would separate the platform from the initial application. You can build a platform that supports a broad range of capabilities, while focusing deployment on one task where there is a clear need. That gives you a way to measure performance, learn from failures, and understand what actually matters to users. Then you can expand to adjacent tasks.

The balance is to avoid making the first application so specialized that nothing transfers, while also avoiding a goal so broad that you never deliver anything useful. General-purpose capability is the destination; focused applications can be the way to get there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think these are two different dimensions: the form of the robot and the generality of its intelligence. A humanoid form doesn’t automatically make a robot general-purpose. You can have a humanoid that does one very specific task, and you can have a specialized robot that handles a wide range of situations within its domain.

The appeal of humanoids is that our environments are built for humans. But that flexibility comes with a lot of complexity. If a simpler robot can solve a customer’s problem reliably and economically, that’s a very reasonable place to start.

My view is to keep general-purpose capability as the long-term goal, but make progress through concrete applications. Pick a task, get the robot working reliably, learn from deployment, and then expand its capabilities. The important question is whether each application gives you something reusable—skills, data, or infrastructure—so that you’re building toward broader capability rather than starting over for every task.
